## 🤖 Claude *(19:18:18)*

<details>
<summary>💭 Thinking Process</summary>

So Playwright automatically injects SwiftShader flags that force GPU rendering through software emulation rather than using the actual virtio-gpu device. This means WebGL and 3D canvas operations run through SwiftShader's software Vulkan implementation, but the CPU still handles 2D CSS rasterization in headless mode regardless.

I'm realizing an important distinction: CSS 3D transforms like `perspective` and `rotateY` aren't WebGL at all — they're Skia compositing operations that apply affine and projective texture transforms on the CPU, which is relatively efficient. That's a key finding separating 3D CSS transforms from actual WebGL rendering.

The chrome://gpu page structure has changed in Chromium 149 with shadow DOM elements, so the selectors I was using don't work anymore, but the WebGL unmasked renderer string is the definitive source anyway. I'll grab the feature status from the page body text directly instead.

Now I'm setting up the probe harness to measure milliseconds per frame for each capability in isolation, with one HTML file per capability using the same scene skeleton and deterministic content.

Building the measurement setup with baseline static cards, then variants adding one effect at a time. I also need to test PNG versus JPEG screenshots since production uses PNG while the benchmark used JPEG — that's a real difference worth measuring. I'll use the reference images from the docs, downscale them to realistic card sizes around 520×320 pixels using ffmpeg, and reference them either as base64 or file:// URLs. Then I'll create a harness that runs through all the variant HTML files and measures frame times at deviceScaleFactor 1.5 with a 1280x720 viewport, testing both PNG and JPEG output formats.

The variants I'm planning: a baseline with just translate animation, then 3D perspective with rotateY/rotateX and translateZ transforms, depth-of-field blur at different pixel values, motion blur using either ghost copies or SVG filters, screen blend mode for glow effects, and a few more techniques to isolate which ones impact performance most.

I'll also render a clean sequence through FFmpeg and apply temporal blending and frame interpolation there to measure the encoding overhead separately.

The key thing

</details>

## 🤖 Claude *(19:36:00)*

<details>
<summary>💭 Thinking Process</summary>

The blur measurements are now showing a clean monotonic progression with low variance, which gives me confidence in the results. The really interesting finding is that 3D rendering with perspective and dolly effects is actually cheaper than the 2D baseline—it's essentially free in terms of performance cost, definitely not the bottleneck I expected it to be.

For blur specifically, the house's claim about 70px blur being 65% of render time was about full-viewport blurred areas, not the card-sized depth-of-field effect I'm testing. The key insight is that the blurred area itself is the cost driver, not just the radius value. On my 4 cards at 64px blur, I'm seeing about a 30% increase. Blend modes like screen and plus-lighter are the real expense at 42% overhead, though the blend mode itself only adds 10 percentage points—the bulk of the cost comes from rendering those large radial-gradient circles. Motion blur ghosts are surprisingly cheap, showing almost no performance impact, but I need to be honest that my test used empty divs rather than actual duplicated card content, which is a meaningful limitation I should address by re-testing with proper ghost replicas.

Now I need to tackle the bigger architectural question of CSS blur versus FFmpeg processing. I should fix the ghost test to include real card content, measure FFmpeg's tblend and minterpolate costs, and compare PNG versus JPEG encoding. I'll start by re-measuring ghosts with actual image content and testing PNG versus JPEG in one benchmark, then run FFmpeg measurements separately using a short rendered sequence to establish baseline and then with motion blur and depth-of-field effects applied.

The key insight emerging is that depth-of-field is fundamentally per-element and per-plane, so FFmpeg can't handle it without a depth map—that forces it to CSS, which costs 5% to 30% depending on radius and area. Motion blur, though, is temporal and global, so FFmpeg's tblend and minterpolate can handle it nearly for free at encode time.

I'm setting up a benchmark to measure this: render 120 frames of the A1 scene at 1920×1080 as PNGs, then encode with the baseline GRADE chain, plus variants using tblend, minterpolate, and gblur to see where the real costs land. The tricky part is that proper motion blur in FFmpeg at 30fps output usually means rendering at higher frame rates and blending down—which doubles the raster cost—versus just blending adjacent frames with tblend, which is cheaper but doesn't add new information.

</details>

<details>
<summary>💭 Thinking Process</summary>

I'm realizing that FFmpeg filters add almost no overhead to the encoding process—in fact, they often make it faster. The baseline encode takes 192 milliseconds per frame, but applying temporal blending drops it to 184 ms because the blurred frames compress more efficiently. Even more complex filters like temporal mixing and Gaussian blur come in at 187 and 173 ms respectively, making them essentially free optimizations that actually reduce encoding time.

The glow effect costs about 21 milliseconds extra through FFmpeg, but doing it in CSS would cost 251 milliseconds—so FFmpeg is roughly 12 times cheaper. The only genuinely expensive operation is motion interpolation at 848 milliseconds, which I should avoid entirely.

The constraint is that FFmpeg filters work globally across the entire frame, whereas depth-of-field requires selective per-plane processing. I could render each plane separately and composite them in FFmpeg, but that would require multiple raster passes and become prohibitively expensive. There might be a smarter approach where I render the background plane once and reuse it.

Actually, the math is clear: rendering in two passes costs an extra 599 milliseconds just from rasterization, which is far worse than the 179 milliseconds CSS depth-of-field would add. So depth-of-field stays in CSS.

Now I need to run the benchmark again with actual content-bearing ghosts and test whether PNG or JPEG encoding makes a difference, since the screenshot encode itself accounts for 70 milliseconds of the total time.

</details>

## 🤖 Claude *(19:50:36)*

<details>
<summary>💭 Thinking Process</summary>

The tmix=5 approach delivers genuine motion blur with the car card smeared along its trajectory, and it's actually more efficient than baseline at 187 ms/frame. The blending also creates a cinematic ghost artifact of the outgoing card, which adds to the visual polish.

That said, tmix=5 on 30fps is technically a very long 166ms shutter exposure — it's over-blurring compared to a proper 180° cinema shutter. The correct approach would be rendering at 60fps with tmix=2 and downsampling to 30fps output, which gives the right shutter angle without the smearing, but that doubles the raster cost. It's a trade-off between visual fidelity and performance.

## 🤖 Claude *(19:56:12)*

<details>
<summary>💭 Thinking Process</summary>

Looking at the benchmark results on an idle host, PNG compression takes 686 ms per frame while JPEG is 369 ms, saving 317 ms per frame or 46%. Since disk I/O is only 4 ms, this is purely CPU-bound compression work. The real engine scene cost is much higher than documented at 686 ms for PNG, which means the worker's 900 ms budget gives only 1.31× headroom instead of the claimed 3×. Now I'm pulling together the key metrics for the final report. Looking at the FFmpeg encoding metrics, blur operations show modest overhead while the glow effect with screen blending is significantly more expensive. The key insight is that the blend mode itself costs around 58ms, but the real expense comes from rendering the three large radial gradients—about 193ms—meaning the bottleneck is the pixel area being painted, not the blend operator complexity. This suggests 3D perspective transforms are essentially free, and performance scales primarily with the area of expensive pixels rather than transform sophistication.

For the specific optimizations: PNG intermediates consume 46% of render time but deliver 10dB better quality than the h264 that follows, so switching to JPEG at quality 95 nearly halves render time with imperceptible loss. Motion blur via FFmpeg's tmix/tblend is essentially free compared to CSS ghosting, which doesn't work visually when ghosts are occluded. The glow effect shows a dramatic difference—FFmpeg's split+gblur+screen approach costs only 21ms per frame during encoding versus 251ms per frame for CSS rasterization, making it 12× cheaper, though it blooms globally rather than per-element like CSS does. Depth of field must stay in CSS since it's per-plane while FFmpeg blur is global, and at 16px the 10% cost is manageable. The minterpolate filter should be avoided entirely due to its 4.4× performance penalty, and without GPU acceleration available, rasterization remains single-threaded, limiting effective parallelization to about two workers on a four-core system.

For a 450-frame Family A scene at 15 seconds, the current PNG path takes roughly 5.9 minutes total, but switching to JPEG cuts the raster time down to 1–3 minutes depending on scene complexity. The optimal architecture splits work between CSS for perspective, depth of field, and masking, while FFmpeg handles motion blur, glow, and color grading. When combining DoF at 16px with JPEG encoding, the per-frame cost lands around 198ms, accounting for the blur delta being roughly similar in absolute terms between formats.

The hybrid approach clocks in at about 413ms per frame with the glow and temporal mix effects, totaling roughly 3.1 minutes for the full clip—about 2.7× faster than the all-CSS approach which would hit 925ms raster plus encoding overhead. I should note though that I haven't actually measured the combined scene with all effects stacked together, so there's some uncertainty in how they interact.

Rather than rely on isolated measurements, I should just build and test both architectures directly—the all-CSS variant with perspective, depth of field, blend glow, and ghost layers versus the hybrid approach with just perspective and depth of field in CSS.

</details>
